Issues connected with this noble verse.

You have learned that the Hijr mentioned in this verse, in His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Hijr did indeed deny the messengers﴾ [al-Hijr 15:80], is the dwellings of Thamud, and that the prohibition of prayer in places of earth-sinking has come. On this occasion we mention the places in which prayer has been prohibited, and we explain what has been authentically established regarding the prohibition and what has not.

The places in which prayer has been prohibited are nineteen, all of which will come.

From Zayd ibn Jubayrah, from Dawud ibn Husayn, from Nafi', "from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'forbade that prayer be offered in seven places: in the rubbish dump (mazbalah), the slaughterhouse (majzarah), the graveyard (maqbarah), the middle of the road, in the bathhouse (hammam), in the camel pens (a'tan al-ibil), and on top of the House of Allah.'" Narrated by 'Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah. Al-Tirmidhi said about its chain: "It is not of that (strength)." Al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated this hadith from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar al-'Umari, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, similarly. The hadith is weak and no proof is established by it, because the first chain contains Zayd ibn Jubayrah, who is abandoned (matruk). Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: "Abandoned." And in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib he said: Ibn Ma'in said: "He is nothing." Al-Bukhari said: "Munkar al-hadith." And he said in another place: "Matruk al-hadith." Al-Nasa'i said: "Not trustworthy." Abu Hatim said: "Weak in hadith, very munkar in hadith, abandoned in hadith, his hadith is not written." Ibn 'Adi said: "Most of what he narrates, no one follows him in it." I say: al-Saji said: "He narrated from Dawud ibn al-Husayn a very munkar hadith," meaning the hadith of the prohibition of prayer in seven places. Al-Fasawi said: "Weak, munkar in hadith." Al-Azdi said: "Abandoned." Ibn Hibban said: "He narrates munkar reports from well-known narrators; so he deserves to be avoided in narrating from him." Al-Hakim said: "He narrated from his father, Dawud ibn al-Husayn, and others, munkar reports." Al-Daraqutni said: "Weak." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "They agreed that he is weak." End of Ibn Hajar's words. And one of the two chains of Ibn Majah contains Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, who was very prone to error; and in it is Ibn 'Umar al-'Umari, whom some scholars weakened, though Muslim narrated from him. Ibn Abi Hatim said in al-Ilal: "Both of them (i.e., the two hadiths) are feeble." Ibn al-Sakan and Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) declared the mentioned hadith sound.

Know first that the places in which the prohibition of prayer has come are the seven mentioned, and prayer toward a graveyard, toward a wall of a latrine on which there is impurity, toward a church and a synagogue, toward images, in the abode of punishment, in a usurped place, prayer toward a sleeper or one who is talking, in the bottom of a valley, in the Mosque of Harm, and prayer toward an oven. The total is nineteen places. We will explain the evidences for the prohibition of them in detail, if Allah the Exalted wills. As for places of earth-sinking and punishment, the ruling on that has already been mentioned just above.

As for prayer in the graveyard and prayer toward a grave: both have been established as prohibited from the Prophet ﷺ. As for prayer in graveyards, there are sound hadiths prohibiting it, among them what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated in their two Sahihs from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): that "the Prophet ﷺ said during his final illness: 'May Allah curse the Jews and the Christians; they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship (masajid),'" warning against what they did; and were it not for that, his grave would have been made conspicuous, but he feared that it would be taken as a place of worship. In both Sahihs there is also something similar from Abu Hurayrah. It is also established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and in some agreed-upon narrations: "May Allah curse the Jews and the Christians," and in some sound narrations, limiting it to the Jews. The Prophet ﷺ does not curse except for an act that is severely forbidden. And from Jundub ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sufyan al-Bajali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ five days before he died, and he was (p-296) saying: 'I disown before Allah that I have among you a close friend (khalil); for Allah the Exalted has taken me as a close friend, just as He took Ibrahim as a close friend. Had I been going to take a close friend from my Ummah, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a close friend. Beware, those who were before you used to take the graves of their prophets and righteous people as places of worship. Indeed, do not take graves as places of worship; I forbid you from that.'" Muslim narrated it in his Sahih with this wording; al-Nasa'i also narrated it.

And from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Make some of your prayers in your houses, and do not make them graves." Narrated by al-Shaykhan, Imam Ahmad, and the authors of the Sunan, except Ibn Majah. His ﷺ saying in this hadith, "and do not make them graves," is evidence that graves are not a place for prayer. Some scholars said: It may be that the meaning of the hadith is: pray, and do not be like the dead in their graves, for they do not pray. Imam Ahmad narrated with a good chain from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), marfu': "Among the most evil of people are those whom the Hour overtakes while they are alive, and those who take graves as places of worship." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it.

The hadiths on this subject are numerous and sound, with no defect in them, and they clearly indicate the prohibition of prayer in a graveyard; because every place in which one prays is called a masjid, since masjid in the language means a place of prostration (sujud). What confirms this is his ﷺ saying in the sound hadith: "The earth has been made a masjid for me," the hadith in full; meaning, every place of it in which prayer is permissible. The apparent meaning of the mentioned texts is general, whether the graveyard has been dug up and its soil mixed with the pus of the dead or not dug up; because the reason for the prohibition is not the impurity of graveyards, as the Shafi'is say, by the evidence of the curse coming from the Prophet ﷺ on those who took the graves of the prophets as places of worship. And it is known that the graves of the prophets, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them, are not impure; so the reason for the prohibition is blocking the means (sadd al-dhari'ah), because when they worship Allah at the graves, the matter leads them to worshipping the graves.

So the apparent meaning of the mentioned texts is the prohibition of prayer near graveyards absolutely, and this is the position of Imam Ahmad; and about its validity according to him there are two narrations, even if its purity is confirmed. Malik held that prayer there is disliked (makruh). The Shafi'is held that if its soil is impure due to being mixed with the pus of the dead as a result of digging, then prayer there is invalid; and if it has not been dug up, then prayer there is disliked according to them. Al-Nawawi reported from Ibn al-Mundhir that he said: "It has been related to us from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', and al-Nakha'i that they disliked prayer in a graveyard." He said: "Abu Hurayrah, Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', and al-Hasan al-Basri did not dislike it." The author of al-Hawi reported from Dawud that he said: "The prayer is valid even if its digging is confirmed." Ibn Hazm mentioned the prohibition of prayer in a graveyard from five of the Companions, namely: 'Umar, 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, and Ibn 'Abbas. He said: "We do not know of any who opposed them," and he related it from a group of the Successors: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Nafi' ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Tawus, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Khaythamah, and others. Al-Khattabi, in Ma'alim al-Sunan, related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he permitted prayer in a graveyard. It is also related from al-Hasan that he prayed in a graveyard.

From Ibn Juraij, who said: I said to Nafi': "Did Ibn 'Umar dislike praying in the midst of graves?" He said: "We prayed over 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with both of them) in the middle of al-Baqi', and the imam on the day we prayed over 'A'ishah was Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar attended that." Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated it. Among those who disliked prayer in a graveyard were Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and al-Awza'i. Those who held that prayer in a graveyard is permissible argued that the Prophet ﷺ prayed over the black poor woman (al-miskinah al-sawda') in the graveyard. The ruling on prayer toward the direction of a grave will come shortly, if Allah wills.

The one who has written this (may Allah pardon him) says: The strongest opinion in this issue, in my view, is the position of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), because the texts are explicit in prohibiting prayer in graveyards and cursing those who take mosques over them, and they are very clear in indicating prohibition. As for invalidity, it is possible; because the prohibition requires invalidity, by his ﷺ saying: "Whoever introduces into this affair of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected." Prayer in graveyards is forbidden, so it is not part of our affair, so it is rejected. It is possible to say: prayer is part of our affair, so it is not rejected; and that its being in the place forbidden is what is not part of our affair.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 15, verse 80 (part 3 of 5):

As is known, there is disagreement among the scholars concerning every prohibited act that has two aspects: one aspect in which it is commanded, such as its being a prayer (ṣalāh), and another aspect in which it is prohibited, such as its taking place in a forbidden place, at a forbidden time, on usurped land, while wearing silk or gold, and the like. They say: if the aspect of command is separable from the aspect of prohibition, the prohibition does not require invalidity (fasād); but if it is not separable from it, the prohibition requires invalidity. However, when they apply this principle, they differ. One of them says: "The aspect here is separable." Another says: "It is not separable," and the reverse. So the Hanbali, for example, says: "Prayer on usurped land cannot have its aspect of command separated from its aspect of prohibition, because the movements of the pillars of prayer, such as bowing, prostrating and standing, all occupy by the worshipper a portion of space that is not owned by him. Therefore the very occupation of it by his body during prayer is forbidden, and so it cannot be an act of worship (qurbah) in any way." The objector, such as the Maliki and the Shafi'i, says: "The aspect is separable here, because this act, insofar as it is a prayer, is an act of worship, and insofar as it is usurpation, is forbidden. So his prayer is for him and his usurpation is upon him, like prayer in silk." It was to this question and the opinions of the scholars concerning it that the author of Mariqi al-Su'ud alluded in his verse:

؎ The entry of a disliked element into what is commanded, without condition or distinction, has been prohibited.
؎(p. 298) So the negation of validity and the negation of reward apply to prayer at a time of disliked [prayer].
؎ And if the prohibition is separable from the command, the act is valid, but reward is not attached to it.
؎ This is attributed to the majority, and it has been said that it is with reward and with punishment.
؎ Invalidity and the obligation to make up [the prayer] have been narrated, and it has been said that only the negation [of reward] applies to it.
؎ Like prayer in silk or gold, or in a place of usurpation, and ablution becomes invalid [in a usurped place].
؎ And a camel-pen, a road, a graveyard, a church, and a place of slaughter for a hot [unclean] thing.

As for prayer toward graves, it is also not permitted, based on what Muslim included in his Sahih, and Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Do not pray toward graves, and do not sit upon them.'" This is the wording of Muslim. In another wording of his also: "Do not sit upon graves, and do not pray toward them." The established principle in the fundamentals (usul al-fiqh, the principles of jurisprudence) is that a prohibition requires prohibition (tahrim). The strongest of the opinions in terms of evidence is therefore the prohibition of prayer in a graveyard and toward a grave, because the bare form of the prohibition, free of any indicators, requires prohibition. As for prohibition requiring invalidity when the act has an aspect of command and an aspect of prohibition, there is the disagreement that we have already presented. If its aspect is one, it requires invalidity. The author of Mariqi said regarding prohibition requiring invalidity:

؎ It has come in the sound [sources] for invalidity, unless evidence comes to indicate otherwise for correctness.

The Prophet ﷺ prohibited, in this sound hadith, prayer toward graves, and he said: "When I forbid you from something, avoid it," and Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. We have already mentioned that his ﷺ curse upon those who take graves as mosques clearly indicates prohibition. Those who held that prayer in graveyards and toward graves is valid argued with evidences, among them the generality of his ﷺ saying established in the Sahih: "The earth has been made a mosque for me," the hadith. They said: its generality includes graveyards. This argument is answered in two respects:

The first: the hadiths of the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition of prayer in a graveyard and toward a grave are specific, while the hadith "The earth has been made a mosque for me" is general, and the specific is applied to qualify the general, as is established in the fundamentals according to the majority.

The second: the Prophet ﷺ excepted from the generality of the earth being a mosque the graveyard and the bathhouse. Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim reported, and the last two declared it sound, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The whole earth is a mosque (p. 299) except the graveyard and the bathhouse." Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in discussing al-Bukhari's chapter heading "Disliking prayer in graveyards," regarding this hadith of Abu Sa'id: "Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy, but there is disagreement about whether it is connected (wasl) or disconnected (irsal). Nevertheless, al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban judged it sound." Al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in Nayl al-Awtar: "al-Hakim declared it sound in al-Mustadrak, and Ibn Hazm al-Zahiri [also did], and Ibn Daqiq al-Id indicated its soundness."

The author of this commentary, may Allah forgive him, says: The verification is that when a hadith is disputed as to its connection and disconnection, and it is established as connected through a sound chain, it is judged as connected, and the disconnection in another narration is not a defect in it, because the connection is an addition, and the additions of a trustworthy narrator are accepted. It is to this that the author of Mariqi al-Su'ud alludes with his verse:

؎ Raising (rafʿ) and connecting (wasl) and an added wording are accepted by the imam of memorization.

From the evidences of those who said that prayer in graves is valid is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "A black woman, or a young man, used to sweep the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lost track of her (or him), so he asked about her (or him). They said: 'She died.' He said: 'Why did you not inform me?' He said: They seemed to belittle her matter, or his matter. So he said: 'Show me her grave.' They showed him, and he prayed over her. Then he said: 'These graves are filled with darkness for their people, and Allah illuminates them for them by my prayer over them.'" In al-Bukhari's version there is no "These graves are filled with darkness" up to the end of the report. They said: this hadith indicates the legitimacy of prayer toward a grave.

Among their evidences also is what the two Shaykhs reported from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to a fresh grave, prayed over it, and they formed rows behind him, and he said takbir four times."

Among their evidences also is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Anas: "that the Prophet ﷺ prayed over a grave."

Among their evidences is what we have already mentioned of the prayer over Aisha and Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the middle of al-Baqi'. These evidences are used to establish the permissibility of prayer toward graves and its validity, not absolute validity without permissibility.

Among their evidences is what al-Bukhari mentioned as a suspended report (ta'liq) from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Umar saw Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, praying at a grave. He said: 'The grave! The grave!' and he did not order him to repeat [the prayer]." End of quotation. Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: "The report of Umar was cited, indicating that the prohibition in this matter does not require invalidity of the prayer. The report mentioned from Umar we have transmitted in connected form in the Kitab al-Salah of Abu Nu'aym, the teacher of al-Bukhari. Its wording: 'While Anas was praying toward a grave, Umar called to him: "The grave, the grave!" He thought he meant the moon. When he saw that he meant the grave, he passed beyond the grave and prayed.'" It has other chains, which I have explained in Ta'liq al-Ta'liq. Among them: through Humayd from Anas, similar to it, with the addition: "Some of those next to me said: 'He only means the grave,' so I moved away from him." His saying "the grave, the grave" is in the accusative in both instances, as a warning. His saying "he did not order him to repeat" is inferred from Anas's persistence in the prayer. If that required its invalidity, he would have cut it off and begun anew. End of his words, verbatim.

The author of this commentary, may Allah forgive him, says: It appears to the observer that these evidences are in conflict. It is known that reconciliation (jam') is obligatory when possible, and if it is not possible, preference (tarjih) becomes obligatory. In this question, both reconciliation and preference are required together. As for the manner of reconciliation: all the evidences mentioned concerning prayer toward graves concern the funeral prayer over the deceased, and none of them includes bowing or prostration; they are only supplication for the deceased, so they are of the same type as supplicating for the dead when passing by graves.

None of those evidences indicates the permissibility of an obligatory or voluntary prayer that involves bowing and prostration. This is supported by Umar's warning to Anas against praying at a grave. Yes, those evidences conflict with the apparent generality of: "Do not sit upon graves, and do not pray toward them," for it covers everything that truly bears the name of prayer, including the funeral prayer over the deceased. The result is that for prayer with bowing and prostration, no evidence has come indicating its permissibility toward a grave or at it; rather the opposite. As for the funeral prayer over the deceased, this is where the evidences conflict. The established principle in the fundamentals is that the evidence indicating prohibition takes precedence over the evidence indicating permissibility. The opponent may say: "A general and a specific do not conflict." So the hadith "Do not pray toward graves" is general, including prayer with bowing and prostration and the funeral prayer over the deceased. The hadiths established concerning the prayer over the grave of the deceased are specific, and the specific is applied to qualify the general.

So the strongest of the opinions according to the methodology of the fundamentals is: the prohibition of prayer with bowing and prostration at a grave and toward it, absolutely, because of the Prophet's ﷺ curse upon those who take graves as mosques, and other evidences; and that the prayer over the grave of the deceased, which is for supplication for him and free of bowing and prostration, is valid, because of the Prophet's ﷺ established action in the Sahih, from the hadiths of Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas and Anas. The hadith of the curse upon those who take graves as mosques points to this reconciliation, because they are places of prostration. The funeral prayer has no prostration in it, so its place is not a mosque linguistically, since it is not a place of prostration.
